runs.prompt: Does the EU AI Act ban facial recognition in public places? Explain the actual rule and cite two real sources. Prefer an official EU source.
runs.answer:
No. The EU AI Act does not ban all facial recognition in public places. It prohibits **real-time remote biometric identification (RBI)**—live capture and matching of people against a database—when used by **law enforcement** in **publicly accessible spaces**. Other uses, such as offline analysis or private security, are not banned by this rule, though they may still be regulated as high-risk AI.

**The actual rule (Article 5(1)(h))**

The placing on the market, putting into service, or use of AI systems for real-time remote biometric identification of natural persons in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited, unless an exception applies [1](https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/24b979fc-4829-11f1-8095-01aa75ed71a1/language-en). The European Commission’s AI Act Service Desk confirms this covers live facial recognition in streets, transport hubs, parks, and similar areas, and that it does not extend to non-real-time or non-law-enforcement uses [2](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/what-systems-are-prohibited-under-article-5-ai-act-eg-social-scoring-emotion-recognition).

**Exceptions**

Article 5(1)(h)(i)–(iii) provides narrow exceptions, including locating victims of crime, preventing a serious threat to public security, and certain substantial public-interest tasks. Any use under an exception requires prior authorization under Article 5(2) [1](https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/24b979fc-4829-11f1-8095-01aa75ed71a1/language-en).

**What remains allowed**

Facial recognition that is not real-time, not remote biometric identification, or not deployed by law enforcement in publicly accessible spaces is not prohibited by Article 5. It may still fall under the Act’s high-risk requirements [2](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/what-systems-are-prohibited-under-article-5-ai-act-eg-social-scoring-emotion-recognition).

**Timing**

The Article 5 prohibitions became applicable six months after the AI Act entered into force [1](https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/24b979fc-4829-11f1-8095-01aa75ed71a1/language-en).

**Sources**

1. [Guidance Study on Article 5(1)(h) prohibition and its three exceptions](https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/24b979fc-4829-11f1-8095-01aa75ed71a1/language-en) — Publications Office of the EU (official EU source).
2. [What systems are prohibited under Article 5 of the AI Act?](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/what-systems-are-prohibited-under-article-5-ai-act-eg-social-scoring-emotion-recognition) — AI Act Service Desk, European Commission (official EU source).

runs.prompt: What changed in the latest iPhone compared with the previous model? Give three changes that matter and cite one hands-on review.
runs.answer:
**iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: three changes that matter**

1. **Variable-aperture main camera** – the main lens can adjust its aperture, giving more control over depth of field and low-light shooting than the fixed lens on the 17 Pro [The Verge’s hands-on impressions](https://www.theverge.com/tech/986400/apple-iphone-18-pro-max-hands-on-impressions-september-2026-event).
2. **Color-matched glass back** – the rear glass now blends more seamlessly with the aluminum frame, reducing the two-tone contrast of the iPhone 17 Pro [The Verge’s hands-on impressions](https://www.theverge.com/tech/986400/apple-iphone-18-pro-max-hands-on-impressions-september-2026-event).
3. **New “Pro” camera controls** – additional on-device controls give photographers more shooting options [The Verge’s hands-on impressions](https://www.theverge.com/tech/986400/apple-iphone-18-pro-max-hands-on-impressions-september-2026-event).
